notes_on_rating: Every theft hypothesis expects the scientist to collect data before she leaves, and H4 can read the same pattern as her copying her own work on the way out. H3 treats the resignation as a coincidence, so it neither predicts nor rules out the download. On its own the item discriminates little.

By itself an unapproved remote tool calling overseas could be shadow IT, for example a researcher working with collaborators abroad, so H4 stays Consistent here and item 6 is where it fails. H2 and H5 make no claim about the tool, which is why they are rated NA.

Two days after the email was opened, the phished credentials were used from a device Aurora had never seen. That contradicts H4's claim that the phishing was never acted on, unless the device proves to be the scientist's own new phone (assumption A4). A journal-portal lure aimed at senior scientists suits both an APT and a criminal crew.

Criminals move stolen data to infrastructure they control, and an upload to the employee's own named cloud account from her own workstation does not fit that, so H3 is Inconsistent. H4 survives this row because the scenario itself offers a policy-breaking backup habit as an innocent reading; item 9 is what undermines it.

evidence_item: 5. No extortion contact or leak-site activity
notes_on_rating: H3 is the only hypothesis that predicts an extortion demand or a sale. The inconsistency is soft, since the window is short and some criminals hold data or sell it quietly. Espionage actors and insiders rarely extort, so silence fits the rest.

evidence_item: 6. C2 infrastructure overlap with known APT
notes_on_rating: The certificate match is the only evidence about who runs the RAT, which makes it the most diagnostic item on the technical side. It counts against a criminal operator (H3) and against an innocent tool (H4). It rests on a single SSL certificate that a second vendor attributed with moderate confidence, and actors share certificates and sometimes plant them as false flags. H2 and H5 make no claim about the RAT.

The move to a rival looks incriminating and discriminates almost nothing. Under H4 it is an ordinary job change and under H2 a career step; H1 reads the rival as a recruitment route and H5 as the beneficiary. A firm in the 'same general region' as the IP addresses is too loose a match to tie it to item 2.

The ACL fault explains how she reached the files and is silent on motive, so every hypothesis that involves her can absorb it. It began about six weeks ago, roughly three weeks before the phishing, so the intruder did not create it.

The file mix is the most diagnostic item on the insider side. A backup of her own work would not contain another project's manufacturing-cost and supply-chain files, so H4 fails. H2 stays Consistent only through its wording about data 'useful at her new employer'; commercial records from someone else's project fit directed collection under H1 or H5 more naturally than career self-interest. H3 does not involve her download.

A footprint of one phished account plus the insider suits a low-and-slow APT and a lone insider alike. Double-extortion crews usually move laterally and escalate privileges before they steal, which makes the row a soft inconsistency for H3. A false alarm would also leave nothing widespread, so H4 stays Consistent. The phished account's anomaly is already counted under item 3.

A regional phishing wave fits H1, H3 and H4 equally, so the advisory confirms little. It does lower the weight of item 3: Aurora was probably caught in a broad campaign, and the phishing's closeness in time to the resignation becomes easier to accept as coincidence.

evidence_item: E12 [ADDED, derived inference from items 2+4]: Exfiltration channel divergence: insider data left through a DLP-visible personal cloud account, not through the RAT/C2 channel already in the division
notes_on_rating: I derived this row from items 2 and 4; the scenario does not state it. A state service with a working implant in the division would rarely let its asset upload through a traceable personal account, so the row counts against the coordinated-insider version of H1. The inconsistency is soft, because services sometimes keep insiders and implants apart on purpose. H3 is left NA so that item 4 is not counted twice.

The tally informs the judgment without settling it. H2 and H5 reach zero partly because they are NA on the four technical items they never try to explain, and H4's three inconsistencies weigh more than H3's four.
